title: The Job AI Was Supposed to Have Eliminated by Now
hook: A decade ago a pioneering AI researcher said to stop training radiologists — the machines would take over. They didn't. The job changed instead, and that pattern is the lesson.
key_points: A prominent AI figure predicted computers would replace human radiologists; Ars Technica reports it hasn't happened.
Reading a scan is only part of the job — consultation, correlation with history, and accountability aren't automated.
AI tools do reshape the work: triaging urgent cases, flagging findings, changing what a radiologist spends the day on.
A confident forecast from a leading expert is still a forecast, not evidence.
The realistic pattern across skilled fields so far: tasks get absorbed, roles get redefined.
content_html: Around the mid-2010s, one of the field's most influential AI researchers offered a memorably blunt piece of advice: stop training radiologists, because computers would be reading the scans within a few years. As Ars Technica revisits the prediction, the striking thing is how thoroughly it missed — radiology is still a profession, still hiring, still central to hospital medicine.
extra_html:
That doesn't mean the AI didn't work. Image-reading models genuinely are good, and they are steadily changing what the job looks like: triaging the urgent study to the top of the queue, flagging a nodule for a second look, handling the volume that would otherwise pile up. What the prediction got wrong was the job itself. Reading the image is one task inside a role that also involves knowing the patient's history, talking to the referring physician, sitting with genuine ambiguity, and signing your name to a call someone will act on. Automate the first task and you reshape the day; you don't delete the person.

It's worth keeping this case in your pocket as a calibration tool. When you next hear a confident claim that a specific profession is finished within three years, notice that this exact claim has already been made, by someone with every reason to know, about a job that turned out to be a bundle of tasks rather than a single one. The safe bet isn't "nothing changes" — it's that the work gets redefined faster than the headcount disappears.

related.title: AI in Healthcare
related.hook: AI can spot a tumor on a scan faster than a tired radiologist and flag patterns no one would catch by eye. It's a powerful assistant to doctors — not a replacement for one.

related.title: AI & Jobs
related.hook: AI is less likely to take your whole job than to take certain tasks within it. The pattern through history: tools reshape work faster than they erase it.

related.title: 15 Million Real AI Chats Say Your Job Is Mostly Fine
related.hook: Google looked at how people actually use AI at work — 15 million interactions — and found that for most jobs, most tasks are simply untouched. The hype is running ahead of the data.

related.title: Hype or Real?
related.hook: AI coverage swings between 'this changes everything' and 'it's all a bubble.' The truth is usually in between — and a few questions help you judge any big AI claim for yourself.

flashcards.prompt: What actually happened to radiology after AI was predicted to replace it?

choices.text: The role persisted but the day-to-day work started shifting
Radiologists were largely replaced, as predicted
AI turned out to be useless for reading medical images

flashcards.explanation_html: Both extremes are wrong. AI reads images usefully and is changing what the job involves — but the profession is still here, because the job is more than image-reading.

flashcards.prompt: Why is 'AI can read a scan' not the same as 'AI can be a radiologist'?
flashcards.back_html: The role also involves correlating findings with a patient's history, consulting with other doctors, handling ambiguity, and being accountable for the call.

flashcards.prompt: What does this story suggest about confident predictions from AI experts?
flashcards.back_html: Expertise in building AI doesn't confer expertise in how an entire profession absorbs it. Treat even a leading researcher's timeline as a forecast to check, not a fact.
